---
title: "Pairwise posterior direction probabilities"
subtitle: "1.8 · the direction probability of two independent normal posteriors, after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024)"
description: "Direction probabilities from the difference of two independent normal posterior variables."
---

Suppose that the true values of units A and B have independent normal posterior distributions. Their pairwise
ordering is described by $\pi_{AB} = \Pr(\theta_A > \theta_B \mid Y)$. This is the posterior probability that A has
the larger true value, obtained by integrating the distribution of A − B above zero. The figure displays this
distribution on the same scales as the two marginal distributions. Independence implies that the variance of the
difference is the sum of the marginal variances, so uncertainty in both true values contributes to the comparison.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .20.** The two posteriors overlap substantially, while $\pi_{AB}$ = .760. The gap is
  measured against the SD of the difference, .283, not against one unit's SD: A's mean is .707 SDs of the difference
  above B's.
- **Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .60 (B much less precise).** The same gap, but the difference widens to SD .632,
  so A's mean is only .316 SDs of it above B's, and $\pi_{AB}$ falls to .624, closer to one half.
- **Means .20 and .20, SDs .20 and .40.** With equal means each direction has probability .500, for either choice of marginal SDs; the difference keeps mean 0 and only spreads out (SD .447).
- **Means 1.20 and .95, SDs .20 and .20 (tutorial sites A and B).** Sites A and B of the six fictional sites in
  postrank's tutorial data: $\pi_{AB}$ = .812. The package stores one minus this number, the chance that stating A
  above B would be wrong.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The formula holds for two independent normal posteriors, set here by hand. For them, whatever their SDs, the larger
posterior mean is always the more likely direction, and $\pi_{BA} = 1 - \pi_{AB}$, because the two true values have
probability zero of being equal. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.E, Example 1, and slide 27 of their talk,
use the special case of this formula with both SDs equal to 1.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank)
1 - pr_tutorial$one$e["A", "B", "score_A"]   # 0.8116204: tutorial sites A and B, one minus the stored error
pnorm((1.20 - .95) / sqrt(.20^2 + .20^2))    # 0.8116204: the app's formula at the same means and SDs
```
:::

Standalone: [embed/two-units.html](../../embed/two-units.html), for example `?muA=.30&sdA=.20&muB=.10&sdB=.60` or
`?preset=equal-means&theme=dark`.
